questions.stem: Outside a bar magnet, magnetic field lines

options.text: leave the south pole and enter the north pole
leave the north pole and enter the south pole
run from the centre of the magnet to both poles
cross one another between the poles

questions.explanation: By definition the direction of the field is the direction in which the north-seeking pole of a plotting compass would point. Outside the magnet that is away from the north pole and toward the south pole, so the lines leave N and enter S. Inside the material they complete the loop from S back to N.

distractorRationale.a: This is the reverse of the agreed direction; a compass north pole would then point toward the magnet's north, which it does not
distractorRationale.c: Field lines do not originate at the centre; they form closed loops through both poles
distractorRationale.d: Field lines never cross; a crossing would mean two field directions at one point

questions.stem: The magnetic field due to a long straight current-carrying wire consists of

options.text: straight lines parallel to the wire
straight lines radiating outward from the wire
concentric circles centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it
a uniform field like that inside a solenoid

questions.explanation: Iron filings or a compass around a long straight wire show concentric circles. The right-hand grip rule gives the sense: thumb along conventional current, curled fingers along the circles. The field is strongest nearest the wire and is not uniform.

distractorRationale.a: Lines parallel to the wire would be the current itself, not the magnetic field it produces
distractorRationale.b: Radial lines describe an electric field around a point charge, not a magnetic field around a wire
distractorRationale.d: A uniform field along the axis is the pattern inside a long solenoid, not around a single straight wire

questions.stem: In Fleming's left-hand rule, the thumb, first finger and second finger represent respectively

options.text: field, current and motion
motion, field and current
current, motion and field
motion, current and field

questions.explanation: Hold the left hand with thumb, first finger and second finger mutually at right angles. The First finger is Field (N to S), the seCond finger is Current, and the thuMb is Motion (the force). This is the motor rule: it gives the direction of the force on a current already in a field.

distractorRationale.a: That order starts with field as the thumb; the thumb is reserved for motion
distractorRationale.c: Current is the second finger, not the thumb
distractorRationale.d: This swaps field and current; using it would reverse the predicted force

questions.stem: A straight wire of length 0.50 m carries a current of 5.0 A and lies perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T. Calculate the force on the wire. Give your answer in newtons.
questions.explanation: With the wire perpendicular to $B$, $\sin\theta = 1$, so $F = BIl = 0.20 \times 5.0 \times 0.50 = 0.50\ \text{N}$. Omitting the length or using $\sin 0^\circ$ would give zero, which is the force only when the wire is parallel to the field.

questions.stem: The magnetic field inside a long current-carrying solenoid is

options.text: zero
strong and uniform, directed along the axis
concentric circles about the axis
strongest at the ends and zero at the centre

questions.explanation: A long solenoid behaves like a bar magnet, but the field in the interior is nearly uniform and parallel to the axis. Each turn contributes a field in the same direction down the middle. Outside, the field is much weaker and loops from the north face to the south face.

distractorRationale.a: The interior is where the field is strongest, not absent; electrostatic shielding of a Faraday cage does not apply to a solenoid's magnetic field
distractorRationale.c: Concentric circles are the pattern around a single straight wire, not inside a solenoid
distractorRationale.d: The reverse is true: the interior field is strong and fairly uniform; it fringes and weakens only near the open ends

questions.stem: The angle of dip (inclination) of the Earth's magnetic field is the angle between

options.text: the magnetic meridian and the geographic meridian
the Earth's magnetic field and the horizontal at that place
true north and the direction of a freely falling body
the geographic equator and the magnetic equator

questions.explanation: Dip is the angle a freely suspended magnetic needle makes with the horizontal, equal to the angle between the Earth's field and the horizontal. It is $0^\circ$ on the magnetic equator (near Nigeria) and $90^\circ$ at the magnetic poles. Declination is the other angle: magnetic meridian versus geographic meridian.

distractorRationale.a: That angle is the declination (or variation), not the dip
distractorRationale.c: A freely falling body defines the vertical, which is not how dip is defined
distractorRationale.d: Those are two imaginary lines on the Earth; dip is a local angle of the field, not the angle between those lines

questions.stem: A wire carrying current lies parallel to a uniform magnetic field. The force on the wire is

options.text: a maximum, because the whole length is in the field
zero, because $\sin\theta = 0$ when $\theta = 0^\circ$
half the maximum value, because $\sin 45^\circ = 1/\sqrt{2}$
directed along the wire, in the direction of the current

questions.explanation: $F = BIl\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $B$ and $I$. Parallel means $\theta = 0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$, so $\sin\theta = 0$ and $F = 0$. Fleming's left-hand rule cannot even be applied in three mutually perpendicular directions when two of the quantities already share a line. Only the perpendicular component of $B$ produces a force.

distractorRationale.a: Length in the field is necessary but not sufficient; the current must also cut the field lines
distractorRationale.c: That would be true only if the wire were at 45° to the field
distractorRationale.d: A magnetic force on a current is always perpendicular to both B and I, never along the wire

questions.stem: A conductor of length 0.25 m carries a current of 2.0 A in a uniform field of 0.40 T. The angle between the current and the field is 30°. Calculate the force on the conductor. Give your answer in newtons.
questions.explanation: $F = BIl\sin\theta = 0.40 \times 2.0 \times 0.25 \times \sin 30^\circ$. Since $\sin 30^\circ = 0.50$, $F = 0.20 \times 0.50 = 0.10\ \text{N}$. Using $\sin 30^\circ = 1$ (as if the wire were perpendicular) would wrongly give 0.20 N; using $\cos 30^\circ$ would give about 0.17 N.
